seo.title: Karmic tail 21 13 10 compatibility: The World, Death and the Wheel
seo.description: Karmic tail 21 13 10 compatibility: The World at the entry, Death in the middle, the Wheel of Fortune as the main task — read through Shakespeare.

title: Karmic tail 21-13-10 in compatibility: a couple in a forest without clocks
short: The 21-13-10 tail in a couple's matrix is built like a riddle: it opens with the card of completion and ends with a wheel that never makes its last turn. The entry to the task is The World: a shared wish to live in a finished world of their own, where time seems to stand still. The middle is Death: along the way the couple loses roles, masks and old pictures of each other, not love. The main task is the Wheel of Fortune: learning to live through the recurring rise and fall without taking each new turn for a verdict.

sections.h2: The story: Rosalind and Orlando in a forest without clocks
paragraphs: Shakespeare wrote the comedy around 1599, and it was first printed in 1623, in the posthumous collection of his plays known as the First Folio. The plot comes from Thomas Lodge's novel Rosalynde (1590). Lodge wrote it on a voyage to the Azores and the Canaries and told his readers that he wrote it "in the ocean, when every line was wet with a surge". A book about a forest world was born at sea. The play and the novel are quoted here in modern spelling.

At the court of Duke Frederick, who has seized power from his elder brother and banished him, there is a wrestling match. Orlando, the youngest son of a dead knight, kept worse than a servant by his own brother Oliver, throws the court champion to the ground. Rosalind, the banished duke's daughter, takes a chain from her neck and gives it to the winner: "Wear this for me—one out of suits with Fortune". Orlando cannot even manage a thank-you.

Soon both of them flee. Rosalind dresses as a youth called Ganymede and goes into the Forest of Arden with her cousin Celia and the court fool Touchstone. Orlando goes there too, with his old servant Adam, and hangs poems about Rosalind on the trees, not knowing she is nearby. Ganymede offers him a strange bargain: come every day and court "him" as if he were Rosalind, and the love will pass. A rehearsal of love begins, with vows and a mock wedding. It ends on the day Orlando is late for their meeting: on the way he has saved his sleeping brother from a lioness, and he sends "Ganymede" a handkerchief soaked in his blood. Rosalind faints, and the game collapses. In the finale Hymen, the god of marriage, joins four couples, the usurper gives up his power, and the exiles go home.

The play moves in three steps, and they follow the order of the tail. First the forest as a whole world where there seems to be no time. Then a game in which the roles die one after another. And finally time, which does arrive in the forest after all — first in the fool's clock, then in Rosalind's own words.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: The World, or a "golden world" without time
paragraphs: The audience hears about the Forest of Arden before seeing it. Charles the wrestler reports that the banished duke lives there with merry companions, that young gentlemen flock to him every day and "fleet the time carelessly, as they did in the golden world". Not the golden age, as one might expect, but the golden world. The first thing said about the forest is that it is a world where time is spent without counting.

In his first forest scene the duke says the same thing in another way: "Here feel we not the penalty of Adam, / The seasons' difference". In the old picture of Paradise it was always summer, and the change of seasons came as the punishment after the Fall. For the exiles the forest is an earthly paradise. Waite sees in The World "the soul's intoxication in the earthly paradise", and it is exactly this intoxication that stands at the entry of this tail.
Then the two meet. The first thing Ganymede asks Orlando in the forest is the time.
— I pray you, what is't o'clock? — You should ask me what time o' day. There's no clock in the forest.

Rosalind replies that in that case there is no true lover in the forest either, "else sighing every minute and groaning every hour would detect the lazy foot of time as well as a clock". And she goes straight on to explain that "time travels in divers paces with divers persons": it ambles with some, trots with others, gallops with others still, and stands still with some. It trots hard with a young maid between her betrothal and her wedding: even if the interval is a week, the week "seems the length of seven year".

The whole tail sits in one exchange. Orlando answers with The World: there's no clock here. Rosalind asks with the Wheel: what time is it? Point M in a couple's matrix is not only the entry to the task but also the "Common language" in the relationship sphere. From the first minute, the common language of these two is an argument about whether their world has time.

In life it looks like this. A couple with The World at the entry soon starts living in "a world of their own": their own words, their own jokes, the feeling that they have met for good. Often that world has a geography too. The two move to another city, build a house far from everyone, or live in two cities and count the days until they meet. The strength of the entry is acceptance: in their own world neither demands that the other become more convenient, and views on life are settled by talking, without pressure. The weakness is the same thing. A world that thinks itself complete takes offence at any clock. Someone else's deadline, a talk about next year's money, a partner's request to change something all sound like an invasion of Paradise. Out loud the two say "everything is wonderful with us", and the hard things are carried out beyond the edge of the forest and never discussed.

sections.h2: The fool's clock: "It is ten o'clock… how the world wags"
paragraphs: In the forest without clocks, only the fool has one. Melancholy Jaques comes running to the duke in delight: he has met a fool in the forest who lay basking in the sun and "railed on Lady Fortune in good terms". The fool drew a dial from his pocket, looked at it with a lack-lustre eye and said, very wisely:

"It is ten o'clock. Thus we may see how the world wags. 'Tis but an hour ago since it was nine, and after one hour more 'twill be eleven. And so from hour to hour we ripe and ripe, and then from hour to hour we rot and rot, and thereby hangs a tale."

Ten is the number of the Wheel of Fortune, the main task of the tail. "The world" is the entry of the same tail. And between them, "we rot": the end, Death. Shakespeare, of course, knew nothing of the destiny matrix, and the coincidence of the number remains a coincidence. But Touchstone describes the mechanism precisely: a world that would like to stand outside time wags all the same, and every hour that ripens it also ages it.

There is one more joke in this speech. Tale and tail sounded the same, and Shakespeare played on it: in Othello the clown says "thereby hangs a tail", and a musician asks back, "Whereby hangs a tale?" And wag, the verb Touchstone uses for the world, is the very word for what a dog does with its tail. The speech about ten o'clock and the world ends with a word that, to the ear, means both "story" and "tail".

Shakespeare did not invent this cluster; it was already in his source. In Lodge, the old servant Adam complains of Fortune: "Thou standest upon a globe, and thy wings are plumed with Time's feathers, that thou mayest ever be restless", and he tells himself that "in the furrows of thy face appears the calendars of death". In our reading the globe is The World, Time's feathers are the Wheel, and the calendars of death are the thirteenth card. All three cards of the tail are gathered in one old man's lament almost ten years before the comedy.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: "not for love"
paragraphs: The lovers' longest scene, in the fourth act, follows the order of the tail. First The World. Orlando threatens to die if Rosalind refuses him, and Ganymede replies: "The poor world is almost six thousand years old, and in all this time there was not any man died in his own person, videlicet, in a love-cause." Then Death. Troilus, says Rosalind, had his brains dashed out with a Grecian club; Leander went to bathe in the Hellespont, was taken with the cramp and drowned, and the historians of the age blamed it all on Hero. "Men have died from time to time and worms have eaten them, but not for love." Then the mock wedding: Celia plays the priest, and Orlando says, "I take thee, Rosalind, for wife." And straight after it comes the Wheel, which we reach below.

What dies in the middle of this tail? Not love but a pose. Orlando has the Rosalind of his poems, hung on the trees. Rosalind has a boy's mask under which it is safe to love. The middle of the task strips away both pictures. Waite opens his account of Death with the sentence: "The veil or mask of life is perpetuated in change, transformation and passage from lower to higher." The mask does not vanish at once; it passes through change.

In the play this happens literally. As he leaves, Orlando promises to be back by two o'clock. Rosalind warns him that if he comes "one minute behind your hour" she will call him the most hollow of lovers, and adds: "Time is the old justice that examines all such offenders, and let time try." Time judged otherwise than she expected. Orlando was late because under an oak he saw his sleeping brother, who had so often tried to destroy him: a snake round the sleeper's neck, a lioness waiting in the bushes. Twice he turns to go — and then fights the lioness. The brother wakes a different man and says of himself: "'Twas I, but 'tis not I." The bloody handkerchief is brought to Ganymede. Ganymede faints and, on coming round, insists it was all counterfeit. A scene later Orlando says the essential thing: "I can live no longer by thinking." The rehearsal is over. This is Death in the middle: the form that was comfortable for the two of them dies — a game in which one knows everything and the other seems to suspect nothing.

There is one more death, and the numbers point to it. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is always the sum of its ends: 21 + 10 = 31, and 31 reduces to 4. Four is The Emperor: power, order, the court. If 21-13-10 were a personal tail, The Emperor would stand between The World and the Wheel. In the couple's tail Death stands in its place. The play does exactly this: the usurper's court, the realm of power and order, ceases to exist in the finale. Frederick leads an army into the forest to kill his brother, meets an old religious man at the edge of the wood and is "converted / Both from his enterprise and from the world", handing his crown to the banished duke. Where a single person would be held together by structure, the couple is held together by a readiness to end an old form.

In life the middle of this tail is made of the moments after which "the old us" is gone. The two move in together, and the long-distance romance ends. Someone leaves the parental home for real, not just for weekends. Jobs change, cities change, the arrangement of "who looks after whom" changes. A partner's past turns up, and it has to be accepted, not rewritten. In its plus, the thirteenth card gives the couple the ability to live through such a change of form without turning it into a tragedy. In its minus it has two opposite faces: clinging to the mask until life tears it off, or turning the change into an "I will remake you" project. Rosalind, incidentally, began with exactly that: she undertook to talk Orlando out of love.

sections.h2: Main task: April, December and the changing sky
paragraphs: Right after the mock wedding Rosalind asks how long Orlando will love her once she is his wife. "For ever and a day," he answers. And he hears:
"Say 'a day' without the 'ever.' No, no, Orlando, men are April when they woo, December when they wed. Maids are May when they are maids, but the sky changes when they are wives."

This is the Wheel of Fortune as the couple's main task. In Shakespeare the line is about men and women, but in a couple each partner takes a turn at being April and December, and gender has nothing to do with it. Lisovskaya names cyclicality as the key to the 10 in a couple: rises and crises follow each other with a certain regularity, and what has to be accepted is the change itself, rather than fought. The main task of the tail is read mostly through its minus, through what the couple fails at. And what it fails at is exactly this: living in seasons when the entry promised eternal summer.

Next Rosalind does something odd and very wise: she announces the weather in advance. She will be "more jealous of thee than a Barbary cock-pigeon over his hen, more clamorous than a parrot against rain", more giddy than a monkey. "I will weep for nothing, like Diana in the fountain, and I will do that when you are disposed to be merry. I will laugh like a hyena, and that when thou art inclined to sleep." It is not a threat but a forecast. The Wheel is hard to bear when every turn is a surprise and a verdict. It can be borne when it is named in advance, like weather. Speaking sincerely, accepting a partner with all their seasons, looking for solutions instead of complaining about fate — these are the tasks of the 10 in a couple, and Rosalind performs them in a single speech.

Let us go back to the duke and his "Here feel we not the penalty of Adam". In the First Folio, the oldest text of the play, it is printed exactly so: "not". The eighteenth-century editor Lewis Theobald decided that "not" made no sense there and replaced it with "but": "Here feel we but the penalty of Adam, / The seasons' difference", that is, here we feel only Adam's punishment, the change of seasons. Ever since, the duke says "not" in some editions and "but" in others. The whole 21-13-10 tail fits into a quarrel over one word. The entry says "not": we are in Paradise, we have no seasons. The main task says "but": the seasons are here, and they are not the worst of it. The duke himself shows at once what to do with winter. When the icy wind bites him till he shrinks with cold, he smiles: "This is no flattery. These are counsellors". And the courtier Amiens answers with a line that holds the couple's whole main task: happy is the one who can "translate the stubbornness of fortune / Into so quiet and so sweet a style".

The minus of this point is familiar to many couples. The swing between "quiet" and "storm" comes round almost by the calendar. The same conversation returns every autumn and every time feels like the end. A dip in money or mood is taken as proof that "we are not right for each other". The grievance is not against a deed but against fate: "we never have any luck". The two wait for the wheel to carry them and let things drift until the upturn is over. The Wheel is neither good nor evil — it turns. The trouble begins when the couple needs someone to blame for the turn.

sections.h2: The clues in Waite and Wen: "The World, or Time"
paragraphs: In The Pictorial Key to the Tarot Waite gives an old list of the names of the Major Arcana. There The World is named in three words: "The World, the Universe, or Time". The card with which the couple enters the task, the one "without clocks", is by its old name Time itself. The forest without clocks and the fool's clock are two sides of one card. Waite also calls The World "the perfection and end of the Cosmos", and he begins the list of Death's meanings with the word "End". The couple has two ends in a row, and after them a wheel that has no end.

The second clue ties the middle to the main task. Among the explanations of Death Waite lists "perpetual movement", and he describes the Wheel as standing "for the perpetual motion of a fluidic universe and for the flux of human life". The thirteenth and the tenth cards are described in the same words. Death in this tail is not the wheel stopping but its turn, seen from inside a single life.

The third clue is in Benebell Wen. She writes: "Many also speculate that the woman depicted on the card was inspired by the likeness of Florence Farr (1860–1917), an English actress, member of the Golden Dawn, and friend to Pamela Colman Smith". So The World of the Waite–Smith deck may well be an actress. And the most famous line of the play runs: "All the world's a stage, / And all the men and women merely players".

The fourth is in Wen too. Her reversed World is, among other things, "the Great Skeptic", the Seeker whose "unusually high intelligence and curiosity causes him or her to question all, and doubt all", and who "finds his or her spiritual fulfillment in that existential ambiguity". The play has such a man. It is Jaques: he delivers the speech about the stage, leads a man's life through seven acts to "second childishness and mere oblivion", and at the weddings refuses to dance: "I am for other than for dancing measures." In our reading The World at the couple's entry splits in the same way: a dancer in a wreath, and a sceptic who watches the dance from the side.

sections.h2: The clues in the numbers: what every 21-13-10 couple shares
paragraphs: The example uses the dates 07.08.1976 and 14.08.1975, calculated by the site's engine. A point of the couple's tail is the sum of the same points in two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The first partner's personal tail is 6-8-20, the second's is 15-5-8. Add them point by point:

The middle is not recalculated from the ends: it is added up from the partners' middles, 8 + 5. This couple's centre is the sum of the personal centres, 4 + 7 = 11, Strength; the couple's values are 6, The Lovers. What follows is what the engine finds in every such couple, not just this one.

**None of the three cards is in the partners' personal tails.** The 21-13-10 tail arises from only four combinations of personal tails: 15-5-8 and 6-8-20 (43% of such couples), 18-6-6 and 3-7-22 (36%), 15-8-11 and 6-5-17 (14%), 18-6-15 and 3-7-22 (7%). None of these seven tails holds The World, Death or the Wheel. Neither partner brings this story along; it is born only between them. Like the Forest of Arden for the lovers: neither Rosalind nor Orlando lived there before they fled, and both came from another life.

**The middle is a meeting of two middles.** Death is made either of The Hierophant and Justice (5 + 8 or 8 + 5, 57% of couples) or of The Lovers and The Chariot (6 + 7, 43%). In our reading, for the first group the old form ends through rules and weighing; for the second, through choice and movement.

**The Wheel is never a plain sum.** The ten in the main task is always reduced: from 28 (8 + 20, 6 + 22 or 11 + 17 — 93% of couples) or from 37 (15 + 22, 7%). In 43% of such couples one partner's personal tail has The Fool as its main task. In the play it is the fool who pulls out a clock showing ten — a coincidence, but a memorable one.

**The centre is Strength or Judgement.** The atmosphere inside the couple is Strength in 64.2% of such couples and Judgement in 35.8%. Strength is the card of a lion mastered without violence. Rosalind and Orlando meet at a wrestling match, and their game is ended by a fight with a lioness. Judgement is awakening and the reunion of a family: in the finale a father recognises his daughter with the words "If there be truth in sight, you are my daughter."

**The values are The Lovers or The Devil.** The Lovers stand in the values of 67.3% of such couples, The Devil in 32.7%. The Lovers are a choice: Orlando twice says "I take thee for wife", once in play and once in earnest. The Devil in its minus is a union with an emergency exit, and the play has one of those too. Touchstone wants to be married by a useless vicar, right under a bush, because "he is not like to marry me well, and not being well married, it will be a good excuse for me hereafter to leave my wife."

**Rarity.** The 21-13-10 tail occurs in roughly one couple in 95 (1.056%) and ranks 34th of the 97 couple tails. No couple tail is made of the same numbers in another order. No one has it in a personal matrix.

**Staying in the forest.** When everyone returns to court, Jaques stays behind: "What you would have / I'll stay to know at your abandoned cave." For a couple this is the world for two turned into a hiding place. There are fewer and fewer friends, everything outside is "theirs, not ours", one evening is like the next, and this is called happiness until one of the two starts to feel cramped. The World in its minus is not open space but the same day on repeat.

**Playing until life tears the mask off.** A rehearsal can last for years. One is always the strong one, the other always the rescued. One always explains, the other always forgives. The roles are comfortable until a bloody handkerchief of their own arrives — an event after which playing is no longer possible. And the mask comes off not at the moment the two are ready for it, but when it is torn away.

**Driving Fortune off her wheel.** In her very first scene with Rosalind, Celia proposes: "Let us sit and mock the good housewife Fortune from her wheel, that her gifts may henceforth be bestowed equally." The wish for a fair wheel is understandable, but in a couple it turns into a hunt for someone to blame for every downturn. And at the extreme it turns into Touchstone's union, of which Jaques tells him, "thy loving voyage / Is but for two months victualled".

ul: **Hanging a clock in their own forest.** A couple needs its own world, but with a calendar: shared deadlines, a talk about money a year ahead, an agreement on what time each of them will be back. Rosalind began love with the question "what is't o'clock?" and she was right.
**Naming the weather in advance.** "I'm hard to live with in November", "when work piles up I go quiet, and it isn't about you". A season announced hurts less than a sudden one.
**Seeing off forms, not each other.** A move, the end of a long-distance romance, a change of roles are marked as the end of a stage, not as the couple's defeat.
**Keeping a reserve for December.** The Wheel's upturn always ends, so strength and money for the downturn are put aside in April.
**Not shrinking the circle.** The Forest of Arden is full of people — shepherds, exiles, a fool. A couple whose world holds only the two of them closes in on itself faster.
**Looking for a solution, not a culprit.** The turn of the wheel is nobody's fault.

paragraphs: The play ends with Hymen's wedding song: "Then is there mirth in heaven / When earthly things made even / Atone together." Atone once meant simply to be "at one". The duke's last words before the dance are "We will begin these rites, / As we do trust they'll end, in true delights." A beginning that looks like an ending is the strong version of the 21-13-10 tail. The couple does not hide from the wheel in the forest and does not wait for the finale; each time it begins the way it would like to end. Its World is no longer a place without clocks but a dance in which time keeps the beat.

ul: **21 · The World — entry to the task.** What the couple agrees on almost without words: "we have found each other for good, we have a whole world for two". It is their common language and their first resistance: a world that thinks itself complete does not want anything in it to change.

**13 · Death — middle of the task.** How the couple travels from that wish to the main task: through the endings of old forms. The game ends, a role ends, a familiar way of life ends, and the two of them remain. This is our reading of the point: in Lisovskaya the middle of the tail has no meaning of its own and only adds to the main task.

**10 · The Wheel of Fortune — main task.** What the couple has to learn: to live in time, where April gives way to December and December to April again, without blaming either fate or each other for the downturns.

intro: This order of cards has a play. In Shakespeare's comedy As You Like It two lovers run away to a forest where, as one of them puts it, "there's no clock". The only clock in that forest comes out of a fool's pocket — and it says ten. What follows is an investigation: the clues in the play, in the books of Waite and Wen, and in the numbers the site's engine finds in every couple with this tail.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 21-13-10 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: These are the tasks of a couple that starts from the feeling of a finished shared world (The World, 21), passes through the endings of old forms — roles, routines, pictures of each other (Death, 13) — and learns to live through rise and fall without taking a turn for a verdict (The Wheel of Fortune, 10). The main point is 10; the other two reveal it.

faq.q: Why does the 21-13-10 tail not occur in a personal matrix?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is the sum of the entry and the main task: with 21 and 10 it would be 31 → 4, The Emperor. In a couple's matrix the middle is added up from the two partners' middles, which is why it comes out as 13. The site's engine found no date of birth with a personal 21-13-10 tail.

faq.q: Does Death in a couple's tail mean a break-up?
faq.a: No. The numbers do not predict events. The thirteenth card in the middle of the tail speaks of a change of form: a stage, a role or a routine ends, not necessarily the relationship. The card neither assigns nor predicts a break-up.

It occurs in roughly one couple in 95, which is 1.056% of all date combinations and 34th place among the 97 couple tails. It arises from four combinations of personal tails; the most common is 15-5-8 with 6-8-20, 43% of such couples.

faq.q: Is there a couple tail with the same numbers in a different order?
faq.a: No: 21, 13 and 10 do not form a couple tail in any other order. The order matters here: the couple starts from The World and arrives at the Wheel, not the other way round.

faq.q: What else should be read in the couple's matrix alongside the 21-13-10 tail?
faq.a: The atmosphere inside the couple — such couples have Strength (64.2%) or Judgement (35.8%) at the centre — and the couple's values: The Lovers (67.3%) or The Devil (32.7%). The World at the entry also appears in the "Relationship and common language" sphere: it is the same point M, so the couple's common language and the entry to its task coincide.

The whole tail fits into a quarrel over one word. The entry says "not": we have no seasons. The main task says "but": the seasons are here, and they are not the worst of it.

The minus of the Wheel is familiar to many couples: the swing between quiet and storm almost by the calendar, the same autumn conversation that feels like the end every time, the endless "we never have any luck". **The Wheel is neither good nor evil — it turns.** The trouble begins when the couple needs someone to blame for the turn. What helps is something else: hanging a clock in their own forest — shared deadlines, a talk about money a year ahead; naming the weather in advance; seeing off forms, not each other; keeping a reserve for December; not shrinking the circle to just the two of them.

The play ends with a dance, and the last words before it are "We will begin these rites, / As we do trust they'll end, in true delights." The strong version of the 21-13-10 tail is a couple that does not hide from the wheel in the forest and each time begins the way it would like to end.

unit.title: A clock in a clockless forest

captions.M: Living in a world of your own, where time seems to stop
captions.N: Seeing off old roles and masks, not love
captions.D: Living in seasons without blaming anyone for the turn

unit.meaning: Your task is to live through the change from April to December and not take a turn of the wheel for the end of love.
